title: Trophic Levels and Energy Transfer
competency: Identify trophic levels and explain the transfer of energy through trophic levels in food chains and food pyramids.
objectives: Define trophic levels in an ecosystem.
Describe the roles of producers, consumers, and decomposers.
Explain the '10% Rule' of energy transfer.
Illustrate how energy flows through food chains and food pyramids.
introduction: Every living thing needs energy to survive, but where does it all start? For almost all life on Earth, the source of energy is the Sun. In this lesson, we will track how that solar energy is transformed into food and passed from one organism to another like a baton in a relay race.
content:
1. What are Trophic Levels?

A Trophic Level is the position an organism occupies in a food chain. It indicates 'who eats whom' and how energy moves.

  • Producers (1st Trophic Level): Organisms that make their own food using sunlight (e.g., plants, algae). They are also called Autotrophs.
  • Primary Consumers (2nd Trophic Level): Animals that eat producers; these are Herbivores (e.g., grasshoppers, cows).
  • Secondary Consumers (3rd Trophic Level): Animals that eat primary consumers; these are Carnivores (e.g., frogs, snakes).
  • Tertiary Consumers (4th Trophic Level): Apex predators that eat secondary consumers (e.g., eagles, sharks).

2. The Energy Pyramid and the 10% Rule

Energy flow is not 100% efficient. When an animal eats another, only about 10% of the energy is stored in its body to be passed to the next level. The other 90% is lost as heat or used for the animal's daily activities (breathing, moving, growing).

This is why there are always fewer lions than there are zebras, and fewer zebras than there is grass. The 'Energy Pyramid' is wide at the bottom and very narrow at the top.

3. The Role of Decomposers

Decomposers like fungi and bacteria break down dead organisms, returning nutrients to the soil. While they aren't always shown as a single 'level' in the pyramid, they are the recyclers of the entire ecosystem.

examples.title: Rice Field Food Chain
examples.description: Palay (Producer) -> Rat (Primary Consumer) -> Snake (Secondary Consumer) -> Philippine Eagle (Tertiary Consumer).

examples.title: Energy Math
examples.description: If the Palay captures 10,000 units of energy from the sun, the Rat only gets 1,000 units, the Snake gets 100 units, and the Eagle gets only 10 units.

keyTerms.definition: An organism that produces its own food (Producer).
An organism that must consume others for energy (Consumer).
The total mass of living organisms in a given area or trophic level.

keyConcepts: Energy flows in one direction: from the sun to producers, then to consumers.
The 10% rule limits the number of trophic levels an ecosystem can support.
Ecological pyramids show the decrease in energy, biomass, and population size at higher levels.
summary: The sun provides the energy that fuels life. Producers capture this energy, and consumers pass it along. However, because of the 10% rule, energy is lost at every step, creating a pyramid-shaped balance in nature where producers are the most abundant and top predators are the rarest.

selfCheck.q: Which trophic level contains the most energy in an ecosystem?
If a plant has 5,000 calories of energy, how much energy will reach the herbivore that eats it?
What do we call animals that eat only plants?
